mainTopic: Coins and their סימנים, items that look deliberately placed (ספק הינוח), a vessel in a garbage heap, and items found in walls
overview: The גמרא asks what the law is when found coins are stacked like the stones of בית קוליס, and a ברייתא rules that the finder must announce them. A second ברייתא teaches that a coin has no usable סימן. Even the claimant's name on it proves nothing, because he may have spent it and someone else dropped it. A new משנה then rules that tied young birds near a fence or on a field path must not be touched. The גמרא explains that they look deliberately placed and have no סימן. Neither the common wing-knot nor the place works as a סימן, since the birds hop. That makes the case a ספק הינוח, and רב rules that such an item should not be taken, but if it was taken it need not be returned. The משנה's rule that a covered vessel in a garbage heap is left alone seems to clash with a ברייתא. רב זביד resolves this by the size of the item, and רב פפא resolves it by the type of heap. The amud ends with a new משנה about items found in rubble or in walls, and a ברייתא saying the finder can claim they belonged to the אמוריים. The גמרא's answer to the challenge against that ברייתא continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: What if coins are arranged like the stones of בית קוליס?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is when coins are found piled in the special three-stone shape of בית קוליס.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the coins were arranged like the stones of בית קוליס, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question about one particular arrangement of found coins. It is setting up the next step, which brings an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Scattered coins look like they fell by accident, so the finder keeps them. The question is whether this specific stacked shape looks like someone placed them on purpose. If it does, the finder would need to announce them.

keyTerms.meaning: A place of idol worship (מרקוליס) where stones were piled in a set shape

phrases.english: Like the stones of בית קוליס, what is the law?
phrases.notes: These are stones piled up at an idol-worship site in a fixed shape. The next step explains exactly what that shape is.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a three-coin stacked arrangement count as deliberate placement, so the finder must announce the coins?

steps.title: A ברייתא rules that such coins must be announced
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says scattered coins belong to the finder, but coins arranged like בית קוליס must be announced. It also describes the shape: one coin on each side and one on top.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as it was taught: If one found scattered coins, they are his. If they were like the stones of בית קוליס, he must announce them. And this is the shape of בית קוליס stones: one here, one there, and one on top of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting a ברייתא that rules on this exact case. The finder must announce coins found in this arrangement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא contrasts two cases. Scattered coins are kept, because they clearly fell by accident. Coins set in a deliberate shape must be announced, because someone placed them that way and the arrangement can identify them.

keyTerms.meaning: He is obligated to announce the find

steps.whatToRemember: Scattered coins belong to the finder. Coins set in the בית קוליס shape (two side by side, one on top) must be announced.

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it was taught in a ברייתא:
If he found scattered coins –
these belong to him;
if they are like the stones of בית קוליס – he must announce them.
And these are the stones of בית קוליס:
one here and one there,
and one on top of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 1 with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Coins in the בית קוליס arrangement must be announced; the arrangement is two coins side by side with a third on top.

steps.title: Claiming a found coin by describing it does not work
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone claims a found סלע by saying it is new, from נירון, or from a certain king, his claim means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who finds a סלע in the market, and his friend meets him and says, 'It is mine, it is new, it is a נירונית coin, it is from such-and-such a king' – he has said nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about someone who tries to claim a found coin by describing it. The ruling is that his description proves nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a person gets back a lost item by giving a סימן, a mark that identifies it. Here the details are ones that many coins share, such as being new or being minted by a certain ruler. So they do not single out this coin as his.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin minted by the emperor נירון (Nero)
He has said nothing; his claim has no legal weight

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who finds a סלע in the marketplace,
and his fellow meets him and says: It is mine,
it is new, it is a Neronian coin,
it is from king so-and-so –
he has not said anything.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Describing a found coin as new, Neronian, or from a certain king does not entitle the claimant to it.

steps.title: Even his name on the coin does not help
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא goes further. Even if the claimant's name is written on the coin, his claim is still worthless, because a coin has no identifying mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: Moreover, even if his name is written on it, he has said nothing, because a coin has no identifying mark.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a bigger חידוש: even a name on the coin is not enough. It then gives the general rule that a coin has no סימן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A name seems like the strongest possible proof, yet it still fails. The ברייתא states the rule that a coin cannot be identified by marks. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even more
An identifying mark used to reclaim a lost item

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the claimant is lying. The point is only that a סימן on a coin cannot prove whose it is right now.

phrases.english: And not only that, but
even if his name is written on it –
he has not said anything,
because there is no identifying mark for a coin.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ שְׁמוֹ כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the ruling of step 3 to the strongest case, a name on the coin, and states the general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin has no valid סימן, even when the claimant's name is written on it.

steps.title: Why a name on a coin proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the finder can say: maybe you spent this coin, and it later fell from someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the finder says: Perhaps you spent it, and it fell from another person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind the rule that a coin has no סימן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Coins pass from hand to hand all the time. Even if the coin was once his, he may have spent it, and the person who actually lost it could be someone else. So the mark shows who owned it before, not who owns it now.

keyTerms.meaning: He spent it (literally, he took it out)

steps.whatToRemember: Coins circulate. A mark on a coin may show a past owner, but it does not show who dropped it.

phrases.english: For he says: Perhaps he spent it,
and it fell from another person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the rule in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin's mark cannot identify the person who lost it, since the coin may have been spent and passed to someone else.

steps.title: משנה: tied young birds near a fence or on a field path
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה teaches that young birds found tied together behind a fence, or on paths in the fields, must not be touched.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If one found tied-up young birds behind a wooden fence or behind a stone wall, or on the paths in the fields, he should not touch them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes young birds that look like they were placed on purpose and rules that the finder must leave them alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tied birds in these spots look deliberately left there, not lost. Picking them up would only take them away from an owner who plans to come back for them.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה; the start of a new משנה

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If he found behind a wooden fence
or behind a stone fence
tied-up young birds,
or on the paths that are in the fields –
he should not touch them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ מָצָא אַחַר הַגָּפָה אוֹ אַחַר הַגָּדֵר
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tied young birds found behind a fence or on a field path must be left untouched.

steps.title: משנה: a vessel found in a garbage heap
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a vessel found in a garbage heap may not be touched if it is covered. If it is uncovered, the finder takes it and announces it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one found a vessel in a garbage heap: if it is covered, he should not touch it; if it is uncovered, he takes it and announces it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case, a vessel in a garbage heap. The ruling depends on whether the vessel is covered or uncovered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A covered vessel looks hidden on purpose, so the finder leaves it alone. An uncovered vessel looks like it fell there by accident, so the finder takes it and must announce it.

keyTerms.meaning: He takes it and announces it

steps.whatToRemember: Things that look deliberately placed or hidden are left alone. Things that look lost are taken and announced.

phrases.english: If he found a vessel in a garbage heap,
if it is covered – he should not touch it;
if it is uncovered – he takes it and announces it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a second case and adds a covered/uncovered distinction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A covered vessel in a garbage heap is left alone; an uncovered one is taken and announced.

steps.title: Why may the birds not be touched?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the reason behind the משנה's ruling about the tied birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the משנה by asking why the tied birds behind the fence may not be touched. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave a ruling without a reason. Usually an אבידה without a סימן belongs to the finder, so the גמרא wants to know why this case is different.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why must you leave alone the tied birds behind the fence from the משנה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה from step 6
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reasoning behind the משנה's rule that the tied birds may not be touched

steps.title: Someone hid them, and they have no identifying mark
steps.stepSummary: The birds were probably put there on purpose. If someone takes them, the owner could never prove they are his, so they should be left for the owner to collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because we say: someone hid these birds here. If a person takes them, the owner has no סימן on them to get them back. So leave them until the owner comes and takes them himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the birds look as though they were placed there deliberately. Taking them would cause a real loss, because the owner has no סימן to claim them with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two ideas work together here. First, the birds are not truly lost, since they were put down on purpose. Second, there is no סימן, so the finder could not return them through an announcement. Leaving them in place is the only way the owner gets them back.

keyTerms.meaning: He hid them or set them down deliberately
An identifying mark used to claim a lost item

phrases.english: Because we say: these, a person hid them,
and if one takes them,
their owner has no identifying mark on them,
therefore, let him leave them
until their owner comes and takes them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The birds were placed there deliberately and have no סימן, so taking them would make it impossible for the owner to get them back. They must be left in place.

steps.title: Why not let the knot be the identifying mark?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that there is no סימן: the knot tying the birds could serve as one.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why? Let the knot be a סימן!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason from step 9. It argues that the birds do have a סימן, since the way they are tied could identify them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the knot counted as a סימן, the finder could take the birds and announce them, and the משנה's ruling would no longer make sense. The challenge targets only the claim that there is no סימן.

phrases.english: But why? Let the knot be an identifying mark!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'no סימן' reasoning of step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the birds have no סימן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The knot is a visible feature the owner could describe, so it should work as a סימן.

steps.title: They are tied by the wings, like everyone ties them
steps.stepSummary: רב, quoted by רבי אבא בר זבדא, explains that the birds were tied by their wings. Since everyone ties birds this way, the knot proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא said in the name of רב: the case is where they are tied by their wings, because everyone ties birds this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The knot here is the standard one everyone uses, so it cannot identify any particular owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סימן must be something unusual that points to one specific owner. A knot that everybody uses is common to all, so it fails as a סימן.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said that Rav said:
It is where they are tied by their wings,
since everyone ties them this way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַב: בִּמְקוּשָּׁרִין בְּכַנְפֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The knot could identify the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks of the common wing-knot, which is not a סימן.

steps.title: Why not let the location be the identifying mark?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: the place where the birds were found could serve as their סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the place be a סימן!
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the knot is ruled out, the גמרא suggests a different סימן: the owner could say exactly where he left the birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An exact location is often a valid סימן. If it worked here, the finder could take the birds and announce them.

keyTerms.meaning: Place or location, here suggested as a סימן

phrases.english: And let the place be an identifying mark!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the 'no סימן' reasoning
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the birds have no סימן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner could name the exact spot where he left them.

steps.title: The birds hop around
steps.stepSummary: רב עוקבא בר חמא answers that the birds hop, so they do not stay in one exact spot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עוקבא בר חמא said: it is a case where the birds hop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the location cannot be a סימן, because these birds move from place to place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the birds hop, the spot where they are found is not necessarily where the owner left them. The place therefore cannot identify the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Where they hop or move around

phrases.english: Rav Ukva bar Chama said:
It is where they hop.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב עוּקְבָא בַּר חָמָא: בְּמִדַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12
steps.terutzMaskana: Hopping birds do not stay put, so their location is not a סימן.

steps.title: If they hop, maybe they came from elsewhere and are permitted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: if the birds hop, perhaps they wandered in from somewhere else and are simply lost, so the finder should be allowed to keep them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they hop, then they came from elsewhere and are permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the answer of step 13 into a new problem. Hopping birds may not have been placed there at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 depended on the idea that someone put the birds there. Hopping undermines that idea, because birds that wandered in are an ordinary lost item without a סימן, which the finder may keep.

keyTerms.meaning: And they are permitted to the finder

phrases.english: If it is where they hop,
they came from elsewhere and are permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a person placed the birds there
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Hopping birds could easily have wandered in, so they are truly lost and the finder may keep them.

steps.title: It could go either way, so it is a doubtful placement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we cannot tell whether the birds wandered in or were placed there. This makes the case a ספק הינוח.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is possible that they came from elsewhere, and it is possible that someone hid them. So it is a ספק הינוח, a doubt about whether they were placed there on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that the birds might have wandered in, but says they also might have been placed there. Because both are possible, the case is a doubt. This sets up the rule in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not claim the birds were certainly placed there. It only shows that we cannot rule it out. The case moves from 'certainly placed' to 'doubtfully placed', and that needs a rule of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: A doubt whether the item was placed down on purpose

phrases.english: It is possible to say they came from elsewhere,
and it is possible to say a person hid them,
so it is a case of doubtful placement,

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר מֵעָלְמָא אֲתוֹ, וְאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר אִינָשׁ אַצְנְעִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reclassifying the case as a doubt
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Hopping birds must have come from elsewhere and are permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both possibilities are open, so the case is a ספק הינוח.

steps.title: The rule for a doubtful placement
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that in any ספק הינוח, you should not take the item in the first place, but if you already took it, you do not have to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא said in the name of רב: in any case of doubtful placement, one should not take the item to begin with. But if he did take it, he does not return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב's general rule for any ספק הינוח. This rule explains why the משנה says not to touch the birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule has two parts. לכתחילה, you leave the item alone, because the owner may come back for it. בדיעבד, once it has been taken, he does not return it. The גמרא does not give the reason here, and it does not spell out what the finder does with it next.

keyTerms.meaning: And if he already took it

steps.whatToRemember: The tied birds are not touched because they are a ספק הינוח with no סימן. The knot is common to everyone, and the place is no help because the birds hop. רב's rule: לכתחילה do not take it, but if you took it, you need not return it.
steps.confusionAlert: 'He does not return it' does not mean he did a מצוה by taking it. He still should not have taken it. It only means that once it has been taken, he is not required to give it back.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of ספק הינוח is a general principle for all found items whose placement is uncertain, not only for birds.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said that Rav said:
Any case of doubtful placement,
from the start he should not take it,
and if he took it, he does not return it.
phrases.notes: The גמרא states this rule without giving a reason.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל סְפֵק הִינּוּחַ לְכַתְּחִילָּה לֹא יִטּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the rule that applies to the doubt identified in step 15
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In a ספק הינוח with no סימן, do not take the item to begin with, but if it was taken, it need not be returned. This is why the tied birds may not be touched.

steps.title: The משנה's rule about a vessel in a garbage heap
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a covered vessel in a garbage heap must not be touched, but an uncovered one is taken and announced.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone found a vessel in a garbage heap: if it is covered, he should not touch it; if it is uncovered, he takes it and announces it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up a new line of the משנה to discuss. This is setting up the next move, where a contradiction will be raised against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A covered vessel looks like someone put it there on purpose, so the finder should leave it for the owner to come back to. An uncovered vessel looks like it was lost, so the finder takes it and does הכרזה.

keyTerms.meaning: He takes it and announces it (so the owner can claim it)

phrases.english: If he found a vessel in a garbage heap,
if it is covered, he should not touch it;
if it is uncovered, he takes it and announces it.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: קשיא (as the first half of the contradiction)
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic of the משנה, after the discussion of ספק הינוח with the birds ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A covered vessel in a garbage heap is left alone. An uncovered one is taken and announced.

steps.title: A ברייתא says a hidden vessel is taken and announced
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that even a hidden vessel in a garbage heap is taken and announced, because garbage heaps get cleared. That seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised a contradiction: if someone found a vessel hidden in a garbage heap, he takes it and announces it, because garbage heaps are usually cleared out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite of the משנה about a hidden vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a covered vessel should not be touched. The ברייתא says a hidden vessel should be taken and announced. Its reason is that the heap will be cleared, so the vessel would end up thrown away together with the garbage.

keyTerms.meaning: And they pointed out a contradiction (between two sources)

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
If he found a vessel hidden in a garbage heap,
he takes it and announces it,
because it is normal for a garbage heap to be cleared out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a ברייתא against the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that a covered vessel should not be touched.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא rules that a hidden vessel in a garbage heap is taken and announced. That is the opposite result for what looks like the same case.

steps.title: רב זביד: big vessels versus small utensils
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד answers that the משנה is about big vessels like containers and cups, while the ברייתא is about small utensils like knives and forks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: it is not difficult. This one is about containers and cups, and that one is about knives and forks. Containers and cups: he should not touch them. Knives and forks: he takes them and announces them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד solves the contradiction by saying the two sources are talking about different kinds of items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that big items like containers and cups would not fall into a heap and get covered by accident, so they were surely put there on purpose. Small items like knives and forks could easily fall in without anyone noticing, so they are treated as possibly lost and must be announced.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the two sources do not really clash

phrases.english: רב זביד said: It is not difficult:
This one is about containers and cups,
phrases.notes: "This one" means the משנה, which said not to touch the item.

phrases.english: that one is about knives and a fork.
With containers and cups, he should not touch them;
with knives and a fork, he takes them and announces them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source deals with a different type of object.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to be about the same kind of hidden vessel.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה deals with large vessels, which were surely put there on purpose. The ברייתא deals with small utensils, which may have fallen in.

steps.title: רב פפא: two kinds of garbage heaps
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says both sources are about big vessels. The difference is whether the garbage heap is one that normally gets cleared out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: both this and that are about containers and cups, and it is not difficult. Here it is a garbage heap that is normally cleared out; there it is a garbage heap that is not normally cleared out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a different answer to the same contradiction, splitting it by the type of heap instead of the type of item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is about a heap that gets cleared, so the vessel is in danger and must be taken and announced. The משנה is about a heap that stays put, so the owner can safely come back for his vessel and the finder should not touch it.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this one and that one

phrases.english: רב פפא said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא וְהָא בְּכוּבֵּי וְכָסֵי, וְלָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Both this and that are about containers and cups, and it is not difficult:
here it is a garbage heap that is normally cleared out,
phrases.notes: "Here" is the ברייתא, which said to take and announce. "There" is the משנה.

phrases.english: there it is a garbage heap that is not normally cleared out.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: הָא וְהָא בְּכוּבֵּי וְכָסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the contradiction in step 18, different from רב זביד's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source deals with a different type of location.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference might have depended on the size of the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with large vessels, what matters is whether the heap is normally cleared out.

steps.title: A heap that gets cleared means the owner knowingly risked losing it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: if the heap is normally cleared, then whoever left a vessel there knowingly let it be lost (אבידה מדעת), so why announce it?
steps.simpleTranslation: A garbage heap that is normally cleared out? That is a loss made knowingly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב פפא's answer, saying his case for the ברייתא does not make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone hides a vessel in a heap he knows will be cleared out, he is willingly risking its loss. That is אבידה מדעת, and in such a case the finder does not have to announce. So the ברייתא's ruling to take and announce cannot be about such a heap.

keyTerms.meaning: A loss the owner knowingly allowed; the finder need not return it

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the ברייתא is wrong. It only says רב פפא's description of the ברייתא's case needs fixing.

phrases.english: A garbage heap that is normally cleared out?
That is a loss made knowingly!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁפָּה הָעֲשׂוּיָה לִפַּנּוֹת אֲבֵידָה מִדַּעַת הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's explanation of the ברייתא from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that the ברייתא deals with a heap that is normally cleared out.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Leaving an item in a place you know will be cleared is אבידה מדעת. That would cancel any duty to announce it, yet the ברייתא requires announcing.

steps.title: The heap was not normally cleared, but the owner decided to clear it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adjusts רב פפא's answer: the ברייתא is about a heap that was not normally cleared, but its owner then decided to clear it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is about a garbage heap that is not normally cleared out, and the owner changed his mind and decided to clear it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes רב פפא's answer so that it escapes the challenge of אבידה מדעת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the vessel was hidden, the heap was a safe spot, so it was not אבידה מדעת. Now that the heap's owner has decided to clear it, the vessel is in danger. So the finder must take it and announce it, as the ברייתא says.

keyTerms.meaning: And he changed his mind about it

steps.whatToRemember: In a heap that stays put, a covered vessel is left alone (the משנה). If the heap's owner suddenly decides to clear it, the finder takes the vessel and announces it (the ברייתא). רב זביד instead splits it by big vessels versus small utensils.

phrases.english: Rather, it is about a garbage heap that is not normally cleared out,
and he changed his mind about it and decided to clear it.
phrases.notes: "He" means the owner of the garbage heap, not the owner of the vessel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 by redefining the ברייתא's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case so the challenge no longer applies.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be about a heap that is always cleared, which would make it אבידה מדעת.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a heap that was normally left alone, which its owner later decided to clear. So the vessel was not abandoned, but it is now in danger.

steps.title: The ברייתא's Reason Fits רב פפא, but What About רב זביד?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's reason, 'because garbage heaps get cleared,' fits רב פפא's answer. According to רב זביד, it seems to have no purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רב פפא: that is why the ברייתא says 'because a garbage heap is usually cleared.' But for רב זביד, what does 'because a garbage heap is usually cleared' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the two answers from before against the exact wording of the ברייתא. It finds that רב זביד's answer does not seem to match the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא made the whole difference depend on whether the heap gets cleared, so the ברייתא's reason is exactly his point. רב זביד made the difference depend on the size of the utensils. So why would the ברייתא mention clearing the heap at all?

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it makes sense (for one view)

steps.confusionAlert: The pattern 'בשלמא לפלוני... אלא לפלוני מאי' is not an attack on the first opinion. It praises the first opinion and challenges only the second one.

phrases.english: Granted, according to רב פפא, that is why it teaches:
"Because it is the way of a garbage heap to be cleared."
phrases.notes: This is the reason given in the ברייתא from step 18.

phrases.english: But according to רב זביד,
what is the meaning of "because it is the way of a garbage heap to be cleared"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to compare the answers of רב זביד (step 19) and רב פפא (steps 20–22) against the ברייתא's wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's stated reason is about clearing the heap. That fits only a size-neutral reading like רב פפא's, so it seems out of place under רב זביד.

steps.title: רב זביד Reads the Phrase Differently
steps.stepSummary: For רב זביד, the phrase means that small utensils often get swept into a garbage heap by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means: because people usually clear small utensils out into a garbage heap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב זביד by reading the same words in a new way. The heap is not being cleared out. Instead, small things get cleared into it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a small change in vowels (לְפַנּוֹת לָהּ instead of לִפַּנּוֹת), the phrase now explains why small utensils were not left there on purpose. They fell in by accident when the house was swept. So they are a real אבידה and must be announced.
steps.whatToRemember: Both answers survive. רב פפא reads the ברייתא as being about a heap that gets cleared. רב זביד reads it as being about small utensils that get swept into the heap by mistake.

phrases.english: Because it is the way of a garbage heap
to have small utensils cleared into it.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁכֵּן דֶּרֶךְ אַשְׁפָּה לְפַנּוֹת לָהּ כֵּלִים קְטַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23 on behalf of רב זביד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase means the heap itself gets cleared, which only fits רב פפא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase means small utensils get swept into the heap by accident, which fits רב זביד.

steps.title: New משנה: Items Found in a Rubble Heap or a Wall
steps.stepSummary: Items found in a rubble heap or an old wall belong to the finder. In a new wall, the outer half goes to the finder and the inner half goes to the homeowner. In a rented-out house, everything goes to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone found items in a rubble heap or an old wall, they are his. If he found them in a new wall: from the middle outward, they are his; from the middle inward, they belong to the homeowner. If the homeowner used to rent the house out to others, then even items found inside the house are the finder's.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives the rules for items found hidden in a heap of stones or inside a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה asks who most likely hid the item. In an old wall or rubble, the owner is unknown and has given up hope, so the finder keeps it. In a new wall, the inner half points to the homeowner and the outer half points to passersby. When many tenants have lived in the house, nobody can be identified as the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: He rents it out to others

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea that where an item is found tells us who probably owns it is central to the laws of lost items.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If he found in a rubble heap or in an old wall –
these are his.
If he found in a new wall,
from its middle and outward – they are his,
from its middle and inward – they belong to the homeowner.
If he used to rent it out to others –

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בְּתוֹךְ הַבַּיִת, הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: even inside the house, these are his.
phrases.notes: 'His' here means the finder's, because so many tenants have lived there.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָצָא בְּגַל וּבְכוֹתֶל יָשָׁן – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the garbage-heap discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items in rubble or an old wall belong to the finder. In a new wall, the outer half goes to the finder and the inner half to the homeowner. In a house rented to others, even items inside go to the finder.

steps.title: ברייתא: The Finder Can Say They Belonged to the אמוריים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains why the finder keeps items found in rubble or an old wall: he can claim they are from the אמוריים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: because he can say to him, 'They belong to the אמוריים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives the reason for the משנה's first rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner of the heap or wall claims the item, the finder can answer that it was hidden long ago by the אמוריים, who lived in the land before the Jews. Since the homeowner cannot prove the item is his, the finder keeps it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Amorites, earlier inhabitants of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught:
Because he can say to him
phrases.notes: The finder is speaking to the owner of the heap or wall, who claims the item.

phrases.english: "They belong to the Amorites."

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁיָּכוֹל לוֹמַר לוֹ שֶׁל אֲמוֹרִיִּים הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind the משנה's first rule (rubble and old wall).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The finder keeps the item because he can claim it came from the אמוריים.

steps.title: Don't Jews Hide Things Too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: why assume only אמוריים hid things? The homeowner could have hidden it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that אמוריים hide things, but Jews do not hide things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'it belongs to the אמוריים' sounds as if only they would hide valuables. But a Jewish homeowner could just as easily have hidden it in his own wall, so the claim seems weak.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a challenge)

phrases.english: Is that to say that Amorites hide things,
and Jews do not hide things?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ אֱמוֹרִים מַצְנְעִי, יִשְׂרָאֵל לָא מַצְנְעִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of the ברייתא in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that the finder can say 'they belong to the אמוריים'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Jews hide valuables too, so the homeowner could have hidden it. The אמוריים claim should not be enough.

steps.title: The Answer Begins: It Is Needed Only in a Specific Case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts its answer by saying the ברייתא applies only in a particular situation.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed only...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line: the גמרא begins its answer, and the details continue on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא צריכא' signals that the ברייתא is not making a general claim. It is talking about a narrow case where the אמוריים claim makes sense. That case is described next.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only (for a specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed only

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא makes a general claim that hidden items belong to the אמוריים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא applies only in a specific case, which is described in the continuation.
